The Story of Bhadrbahu Muni

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who brings welfare to the world and is worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of the fifth Shrut-Kevali, Shri Bhadrbahu Muni, which brings welfare to all.

In the land of Pundravardhan, in the city of Kotipur, during the reign of King Padmarath, there lived a priestly Brahmin named Somsharma. His wife was Shridevi. The hero of this story, Bhadrbahu, was their son. From childhood, Bhadrbahu was peaceful and grave in nature. Looking at his auspicious face, one could easily imagine that he would grow up to be some great, famous soul. For the saying is entirely true: "The feet of the destined child are seen in the cradle itself."

When Bhadrbahu was eight years old and had undergone the sacred thread ceremony, one day he was playing marbles with his companions. Each child showed their skill by stacking marbles one on top of another. Some stacked two, some four, some six, and a few clever ones managed eight. But our hero Bhadrbahu surpassed them all. He stacked fourteen marbles in a single tower! All the children were amazed.

At that very moment, an event occurred. Shri Govardhanacharya, the fourth Shrut-Kevali among the fourteen who know the Maha-purvas, was travelling to Girnar. He was one of the five great Shrut-Kevalis who would follow Lord Vardhaman's nirvana. Seeing Bhadrbahu's astonishing skill in stacking marbles, he understood through his knowledge of omens that this child must be the one destined to become the fifth Shrut-Kevali. Upon learning Bhadrbahu's name and details, his conviction grew stronger. He took Bhadrbahu to his home and asked Somsharma for permission to teach him. Somsharma, without hesitation, entrusted his son to the Acharya.

The Acharya took Bhadrbahu to his place and taught him thoroughly, making him a model scholar in all subjects. When the Acharya saw that Bhadrbahu had become a fine scholar, he sent him back home — lest Somsharma think that the Acharya had led his son astray to become a monk. Bhadrbahu returned home, but his heart was no longer in worldly life.

Through the ripening of merit, Bhadrbahu soon took initiation as a monk. He studied the fourteen Maha-purvas and mastered all the scriptures. He became the fifth Shrut-Kevali — one who knows all the Jain scriptures in their entirety. Through his vast knowledge and saintly conduct, he brought countless souls to the path of dharma. He composed many works that illuminated the teachings of the Jinas and guided generations of seekers.

Ultimately, through dedicated spiritual practice, Bhadrbahu Muni destroyed his karmas and attained liberation.

This story teaches that great destiny manifests even in childhood. Bhadrbahu's extraordinary skill with marbles was a sign of the great scholar he would become. But destiny alone is not enough — he had to study diligently and practise austerities to fulfil that destiny. The wise should nurture the talents of children and guide them toward both worldly learning and spiritual wisdom.
